authors.name: Rowan Vale
authors.bio: The man behind The Pecking Order. Rowan trades in sharp verdicts, spectacular reversals and an unwavering belief that this week finally explained everything. His inbox rarely agrees.

authors.name: Mara Voss
authors.bio: Mara follows the details that outlast the scoreboard: protection, personnel, responsibility and the choices that turn a talented roster into a contender.

authors.name: Ellis Quill
authors.bio: Ellis writes The Long Season, a column about the people and expectations beneath the standings. A bad afternoon is evidence, not a complete biography.

authors.name: Dorian Pike
authors.bio: Dorian asks the awkward question, counts the points and keeps asking. The Uncomfortable Truth takes the league’s overlooked clubs seriously.

authors.name: Tessa Wren
authors.bio: Tessa studies the matchups, names the pressure points and puts a score beside every pick. She covers the entire weekly slate for The Week Ahead.

authors.name: Calvin Rook
authors.bio: Calvin covers the college game and the next IFL class. The Rook Board is built around projection, athletic traits and the occasional prospect he refuses to stop believing in.

articles.title: Eighty yards to stay unbeaten
articles.dek: Accel BeckhmJr caught the winner, Electric Berry took away the answer, and Mossdeep survived Saffron 20–17. A second-half shutout came with a painful cost: Marshall Flock is out five weeks.
articles.author: mara-voss

body.text: Mossdeep had to play another fourth quarter that could spoil everything. Good. After the recent blowouts, I wanted to see what this offense would do when the next touchdown was necessary, the opposing pass rush had already made its point, and the running back couldn't spend the afternoon collecting short scores. The answer was an eighty-yard drive, Accel BeckhmJr in the end zone with forty-nine seconds left, and a 20–17 victory over Saffron.

That doesn't make the first half disappear. The Eclipse trailed 17–6 at the break. Medicham sacked Dram Marino four times, all before the middle of the third quarter. Saffron had the more productive passing afternoon and finished with a 334–314 advantage in total yards. This was a difficult opponent playing well enough to win. Mossdeep stayed unbeaten because it eventually completed the work its first-half possessions had left unfinished, while its defense stopped allowing Saffron to finish anything.

Michael Dorrill's team is 9–0. Trent Scarboro's Psi Corps fell to 7–2, their seven-game winning streak over. BeckhmJr caught eight passes for 117 yards and both Eclipse touchdowns. Electric Berry recovered a fumble, then intercepted Archam Manning's first throw after the winning score. Those two players supply the clean headline. Marshall Flock's five-week injury supplies the part nobody can celebrate away.
I would've preferred to make everybody comfortable a little earlier. Apparently we were doing suspense this week. Dram kept coming back to me, and the last one was the one we had to have.
body.speaker: Accel BeckhmJr

body.text: Saffron made the early possessions count

The visitors' first touchdown required actual work: nine plays and eighty yards. Manning converted third-and-seven with a deep-left throw to Dam Skattebo for twenty-four yards, then third-and-eight with a nine-yard short-left completion to Gengar Pickens. On the next snap he went deep left to Pickens again, this time for a thirty-yard touchdown with forty seconds left in the opening quarter. The scoring play was the reward for surviving the two difficult downs before it.

Mossdeep responded with a long possession of its own. BeckhmJr converted third-and-ten for twenty-seven yards; Lorenzo Steel later gained sixteen on third-and-four. Then Medicham sacked Marino for six yards, and the drive stalled. Adam Vinathorn's forty-yard field goal made it 7–3. I liked the conversions. I disliked the ending. Against Saffron, driving close enough to admire the end zone was not going to be sufficient.

The Psi Corps went seventy-five yards in eleven plays on their next possession. Skattebo and Emmitt Smoth contributed useful runs, Gorebyss caught two passes, and Manning spread the ball without giving the drive away. Pawmo caught the three-yard touchdown on a short-left throw with 1:22 remaining in the half. Saffron had twice built a touchdown drive of at least seventy-five yards. It wasn't living on one fortunate bounce.

Ninjulio Jones' forty-four-yard kickoff return gave Mossdeep a chance to answer quickly. Instead, Medicham recorded consecutive sacks, losses of seven and five yards. Gronkaludon's eighteen-yard catch on third-and-twenty-two salvaged kicking range, and Vinathorn's forty-seven-yarder went in off the upright. The kicker had six points. The offense had two separate reasons to thank him.

Saffron still found time for a seventy-yard drive and Vikavolt's twenty-seven-yard field goal. Pickens supplied the biggest gain, forty-eight yards down the left side with eighteen seconds on the clock. Manning went to halftime with the lead and evidence that Mossdeep's secondary could be stretched. Pickens finished with four catches for 107 yards. Any account that turns Saffron into an undeserving loser has misplaced the entire first half.
We put ourselves in position to finish a good win. In the second half we kept asking the defense to get us another stop. Eventually we had to give it something back, and we didn't.
body.speaker: Trent Scarboro

body.text: The comeback began with stops

The Eclipse did not emerge from halftime with an instant offensive cure. Their first two possessions ended in punts. Medicham collected his fourth sack on the second, dropping Marino for six yards on third-and-seven. He finished with nine pressures as well as those four sacks. Verrick Brooks' absence did not leave Saffron without a disruptive linebacker. Medicham was the best argument against that assumption all afternoon.

Mossdeep's defense bought the offense time. Saffron's first two second-half possessions also ended in punts, gaining one yard and six yards respectively. Ray Glewis broke up a short throw on the first series. Luvrelle Revis limited a Skattebo run to one yard. On the next, Joey Sporeter and Ronnie Watt made the tackles before Manning threw the ball away on third-and-four. Those are small events until the offense needs six more chances to get itself organized.

The first Eclipse touchdown finally arrived on a six-play, sixty-seven-yard drive. Steel caught a sixteen-yard short-right pass. BeckhmJr followed with thirty-two yards deep right and eleven more short right. After a Ninjaskamara run and an incompletion, Marino found BeckhmJr short left for five yards on third-and-five. At 17–13, with 1:37 left in the third quarter, the game had become manageable without becoming comfortable.

Then the teams exchanged the sort of opportunities that make coaches repeat themselves. Armaldo Pace sacked Manning for eight yards. Later in that possession, Skattebo fumbled and Berry recovered. Two plays after Mossdeep took over, Richard Furman fumbled on a run up the middle, with Octillery recovering for Saffron. Nobody earned a touchdown from the exchange. The Eclipse had gained a chance and immediately returned it.

The defense answered again. Shawn Mareman sacked Manning for five yards near the end of the third quarter. Glewis stopped Skattebo for a three-yard loss to open the fourth. Druddamukong then sacked Manning for eight more on third-and-eighteen. That sequence erased the value of Saffron's recovery. Mossdeep's offense could be frustrated with itself while still receiving another possession within one score.
The fumble was Ronnie's work before it was mine. I just tried to be there. On the interception, I saw the throw and got to it. It's easier talking about it after the clock stops.
body.speaker: Electric Berry

body.text: The drive that mattered used both halves of the offense

Saffron's last serious chance to protect the lead began with Mothel Irving's thirty-two-yard catch. It reached another third down, but Manning's deep-right throw to Pickens fell incomplete on third-and-eight. Vikavolt punted into the end zone. Mossdeep took over at its twenty with 1:48 left, trailing by four. A field goal would have been useful earlier. It was no longer the assignment.

Marino opened with two throws to Ninjaskamara: seven yards short right, then nineteen deep left. BeckhmJr gained twenty-two more on a deep-right completion. Those three catches moved the drive quickly, but Dorrill's offense didn't turn the rest into a frantic throwing contest. Ninjaskamara carried four consecutive times, gaining four, ten, ten and two yards. The back who finished with seventy-eight rushing yards made twenty-six of them count on this possession.

On second-and-six, with forty-nine seconds showing, Marino went short right to BeckhmJr for the touchdown. Vinathorn added the extra point. Marino finished seventeen-of-twenty-six for 218 yards, two touchdowns and no interceptions. He had endured four sacks and several stalled possessions. When Mossdeep needed an eighty-yard answer, he completed all four passes on the drive, and Ninjaskamara kept the running game fully involved.

Saffron's response lasted one throw. Manning went deep left; Berry intercepted and returned it five yards. The quarterback's final line was twenty completions in twenty-eight attempts for 258 yards, two touchdowns and that one interception. It was a good afternoon with a disastrous final entry. Mossdeep still had to close the game, which Furman helped do with an eight-yard run right on third-and-two with thirty-nine seconds remaining.

The health report complicates the celebration. Flock is out five weeks. BeckhmJr has a minor injury entry with no remaining absence. Mossdeep now goes to Vermilion at 9–0; Saffron hosts Fortree at 7–2. The Eclipse have shown they can survive a contender's best stretch. Now they must replace a corner while preserving what worked after halftime. For this week, the final defensive instruction was fulfilled exactly: Manning threw, Berry caught it, and Saffron never got another snap.

articles.title: Five touchdown passes, three Timmy scores, and one last exhale
articles.dek: Rustboro held off Cinnabar 41–38 after a fourth quarter that produced forty-two points. Gibby Timmy dominated through the air; Philly supplied the final first down.
articles.author: tessa-wren

body.text: Rustboro's best offensive play of the closing two minutes was a run. That may seem an odd place to begin a game in which Porygon-Z threw five touchdown passes and Gibby Timmy caught three, but the Stone had already demonstrated how quickly they could score. What they needed at the end was to prevent Cinnabar from getting another turn. Philly ran right for eleven yards on second-and-six. Porygon-Z knelt twice. A 41–38 win could finally be filed without adding another scoring entry.

The Stone improved to 6–4 with their third consecutive victory. Cinnabar fell to 7–3 despite scoring twenty-eight points in the fourth quarter and outgaining Rustboro 405–377. Porygon-Z completed sixteen of twenty-five throws for 268 yards, five touchdowns and one interception. Timmy caught seven passes for 157 yards, with touchdown receptions of thirty-three, ten and forty-six yards. He also returned a kickoff seventy-five yards to create another score. Cinnabar's pass defense and kick coverage both struggled to contain him.

Tyler Scarboro's team led 20–3 at halftime and 27–10 after three quarters. Neither lead survived as a comfortable arrangement. The final period included two one-play Stone touchdown drives, a ninety-seven-yard Cinnabar kickoff-return touchdown, three failed Blaze onside kicks, a missed extra point and a successful two-point conversion. The scoreboard was busy enough. The closing first down was a welcome change of subject.

I liked the part where they had to kick it to us again. That's another chance to make the afternoon irritating. Three touchdowns is nice, but getting that last first down saved us from having to find a fourth.
body.speaker: Gibby Timmy

body.text: Rustboro built the lead before the fireworks

The opening possessions were comparatively ordinary. Gorebyss made a forty-two-yard field goal. Tatsugiri intercepted Porygon-Z's next first-down throw, and Charjabug's twenty-nine-yarder tied the game at three. Rustboro limited the cost of its early turnover to a field goal. Cinnabar had tied the score, but its offense had finished another possession short of the end zone.

Rustboro's first touchdown drive supplied the foundation for everything that followed: twelve plays, seventy-six yards and repeated ground work. My Way, Son began it with a sixteen-yard run. Philly carried the middle of the possession, including an eight-yard gain up the middle on fourth-and-one. He converted another short situation before Porygon-Z found Lombre short left for a five-yard touchdown with 3:04 left in the second quarter. For a team about to produce so many explosive passes, the willingness to sustain this drive mattered.

Seismitoad fumbled on Cinnabar's ensuing possession. Smoke Break recovered, and the Stone added Gorebyss' thirty-three-yard field goal. The offense gained only two yards after the takeaway, so this was not a perfect exploitation of the chance. It still moved the score to 13–3. Cinnabar then punted again, leaving Rustboro another late-half opportunity with a lead already established.

Porygon-Z needed four plays to cover sixty-six yards. Gengar caught an eleven-yard pass; SEARED BITE followed with twenty-two yards down the left side. An incompletion preceded Timmy's thirty-three-yard touchdown on a deep-right throw with 1:03 left. The Stone took a seventeen-point advantage into halftime. They had scored through a long ground-based possession, a short field after a turnover, and a quick passing drive. Cinnabar had several different problems to address.
The long drive mattered as much as the quick ones. Philly kept us moving when we had to earn the next down. At the end we needed the same thing again: keep the ball, get the first down, finish.
body.speaker: Tyler Scarboro

body.text: Timmy kept finding the expensive answer

Cinnabar began the second half with a three-play, seventy-three-yard touchdown drive. Gholdengo's sixty-one-yard deep-right completion to Exploud set up Seismitoad's nine-yard scoring run left. It was an immediate reminder that the Blaze could move the game in large pieces too. The margin fell to ten, and Rustboro's next possession ended in a punt. At that point the comeback was more than an abstract possibility.

The Stone defense forced a punt on Cinnabar's next series. Rustboro then traveled seventy-seven yards in seven plays, surviving two third downs through the air. SEARED BITE gained fifteen on third-and-nine. Timmy gained forty-eight on third-and-seven, then caught a ten-yard deep-right touchdown on the very next snap. Those consecutive catches explain his afternoon more clearly than a general claim about speed: he supplied the drive's longest gain and immediately finished the opportunity it created.

SEARED BITE's forty-eight receiving yards deserve to remain in the account alongside Timmy's larger total. The fifteen-yard third-down catch prevented the series from ending before the forty-eight-yard play. Gengar added three catches for fifty-six yards and a touchdown, while Lombre's single target became the first Stone touchdown. Porygon-Z used the supporting receivers well enough that Cinnabar could not solve the game merely by acknowledging who was having the biggest day.

The quarterback also went the entire afternoon without being sacked. So did Gholdengo. This was a game decided through completions, coverage, returns and finishing rather than one quarterback repeatedly retreating under pressure. Cinnabar's passer attempted forty-five throws and completed twenty-seven for 325 yards, two touchdowns and no interceptions. Those numbers were substantial. Rustboro's five passing touchdowns were more immediately valuable.
We had the time to find the next throw. The receivers finished the chances. Late in the game I wanted the ball to stay with us. Philly made that simple.
body.speaker: Porygon-Z

body.text: Forty-two fourth-quarter points did not change the winner

Seismitoad's three-yard rushing touchdown early in the fourth quarter brought Cinnabar within ten again. Timmy returned the kickoff seventy-five yards to the Blaze nineteen. Porygon-Z promptly found Gengar deep over the middle for a nineteen-yard touchdown. Rustboro's offense had used one snap to restore the seventeen-point margin. Timmy's contribution to that score did not appear in his receiving total, but it was plainly visible in the starting field position.

Gholdengo answered with an eight-play, eighty-two-yard drive, ending in an eight-yard short-right touchdown to Skiploom. Charjabug missed the extra point wide left. The Blaze tried an onside kick; SEARED BITE recovered at the Cinnabar forty-six. On the next snap, Porygon-Z went deep left to Timmy for all forty-six yards. Gorebyss' extra point put Rustboro ahead 41–23 with 3:52 remaining. That looked like enough separation. It lasted for one kickoff.

Archaludon took that kickoff ninety-seven yards for a touchdown. Cinnabar was back within eleven after the extra point. The Blaze tried another onside kick, which Aggron recovered for Rustboro. This time the Stone did not convert the short field into points. Two incomplete throws to SEARED BITE followed a short run, and Gorebyss punted into the end zone. Cinnabar had the ball back with 3:04 left, needing two scores and receiving another opportunity to make everyone uncomfortable.

Gholdengo moved the Blaze eighty yards in eleven plays. Frogadier supplied catches of nineteen and nine yards. Buizel added twelve and eighteen. Mawile caught a seven-yard short-left pass, then scored from four yards on third-and-three. Seismitoad ran up the middle for the two-point conversion. The score was 41–38 with 1:51 remaining, and Rustboro's eighteen-point lead had become a three-point problem.

Pupitar recovered Cinnabar's third onside attempt. Porygon-Z found Timmy short right for four yards, and Philly followed with the eleven-yard run that allowed the kneels. The Blaze never received the final possession they had spent the quarter trying to manufacture. They produced more first downs and more yards than Rustboro, but the Stone recovered every onside attempt and kept the last meaningful series in their own hands.

Cinnabar's 38 points were its best argument and its most frustrating number: enough offense to win many afternoons, insufficient compensation for five touchdown passes allowed. Rustboro can enjoy the victory while reviewing how a 41–23 lead became a live contest. Both clubs have a Week 11 bye. My Way, Son is listed out one week; his thirty-nine rushing yards came on five carries, while Philly finished with sixty-six on seventeen. The break arrives with the Stone fifth in the current Hoenn–Sinnoh playoff order and the Blaze fourth in Kanto–Johto. For Rustboro, the useful closing picture is still Philly going right, eleven yards gained, and the passing show finally allowed to end.

articles.title: The Reds leave no invitation: 34–0, and nine straight
articles.dek: Tic Thorpe accounted for four touchdowns as Mt. Silver returned from its bye, collected four Canalave turnovers and stayed unbeaten. Six catches on six targets made Scep Smith Jr. the drive-saving constant.
articles.author: rowan-vale

body.text: Canalave had a respectable record, a useful defense and the visitors coming off a week without a game. Mt. Silver responded by treating every loose ball as a delivery addressed to the Reds. Four Bulwark turnovers became twenty points, Tic Thorpe accounted for four touchdowns, and a 34–0 road win moved Connor McLarren's team to 9–0. The welcome-back party was rather one-sided. Canalave apparently supplied the gifts.

Thorpe threw for 281 yards and three touchdowns, completing twenty-one of thirty-three passes without an interception. He added a one-yard rushing score. The Reds outgained the Bulwark 366–154, converted seven of thirteen third downs, and held Canalave to seven first downs. Mt. Silver now has 239 points scored and 68 allowed. The undefeated record is eye-catching; the repeated refusal to let opponents assemble an answer is what makes it persuasive.

There were enough contributors to prevent this from becoming a quarterback biography. Scep Smith Jr. caught all six of his targets for sixty-four yards. Tony Gyarzalez caught five passes for seventy-seven and a touchdown. Gregar Jenings caught all three of his targets for fifty-three and a score. Tentacool added fifty yards and a touchdown. Tauros Woodson intercepted a pass and recovered a fumble. Kevin Metwae recovered two fumbles, including one that kept an early Reds possession alive. Everybody seemed to have been assigned a useful errand.
If it's on the ground, I'm going after it. We recovered ours, then we recovered theirs. You don't need a complicated explanation for why that helps.
body.speaker: Kevin Metwae

body.text: An early escape became an immediate touchdown

Mt. Silver's opening possession was not an immaculate demonstration. Raticate fumbled on the second play, and Metwae recovered. Delcatty then sacked Thorpe for seven yards. The Reds eventually punted after two Vibrava runs failed to undo the lost ground. Canalave had forced the stop it needed. Then Sneasel fumbled on the punt return, and Metwae recovered again, this time giving his offense the ball in scoring position.

Thorpe needed one play. He threw deep right to Jenings for a twenty-three-yard touchdown with 4:12 left in the first quarter. Two fumbles had occurred, but only Canalave's changed possession. The difference between keeping the first one and taking the second was a seven-point lead. Metwae's busy few minutes deserve more than a quiet note beneath the passing totals.

The Bulwark moved the ball on the ground during their first offensive series. Gabite gained six, one, five and four yards on consecutive carries. Then two Deerling runs lost a combined three yards, and Canalave punted. Those first four carries were encouraging enough to show a path. The next two showed how quickly that path could narrow when the offense needed another conversion.

Mt. Silver answered with a proper long drive, seventy-six yards in eight plays. Gyarzalez opened with an eight-yard reception. Jenings moved the chains, Smith gained fourteen on third-and-four, and Plusico Buress caught a nineteen-yard deep-left pass. With three seconds left in the quarter, Thorpe found Gyarzalez deep right for a nineteen-yard touchdown. The Reds had scored from a turnover-created short field and then from their own twenty-four. Canalave could not blame the whole deficit on the return mishap.

The recoveries gave us opportunities. The next job was to make those opportunities count, and the offense did that. We also had long drives where we earned the field ourselves. I liked that we could do both.
body.speaker: Connor McLarren

body.text: The completions that kept the afternoon moving

Smith's perfect six-for-six receiving line was not decorative efficiency. His fourteen-yard catch kept the second touchdown drive alive. In the second quarter he converted third-and-eight with nine yards. Later he supplied gains of ten and thirteen to help the Reds continue moving. There were no enormous numbers attached to any one catch, which is precisely why a defense can spend an afternoon feeling that it is almost off the field and still never get there.

Canalave's first pass of the second quarter made that problem worse. Slowking went deep left, and Woodson intercepted, returning the ball fourteen yards. Mt. Silver's offense gained seven yards on the ensuing series, enough for Adam Venutieri to make a fifty-three-yard field goal. It was 17–0. The Reds had turned their first two takeaways into ten points without asking either possession to be especially long.

The next Reds drive came close to adding more. Thorpe converted third downs to Smith and Jenings, then found Vulpix for another first down. Three consecutive incompletions toward Nuzleaf stopped the progress, the last two broken up by Weezing and Medicham. Canalave then produced a special-teams answer. Froslass blocked Venutieri's thirty-one-yard attempt with forty-eight seconds left in the half. A defense still waiting for its offense to score had at least kept three more points away.

Canalave promptly lost the ball again. Slowking was sacked and fumbled with twenty-seven seconds remaining, and Scizor recovered for Mt. Silver. Thorpe found Gyarzalez for five yards and Tentacool for twenty-one on third-and-five. Venutieri made a twenty-yard field goal with seven seconds left. The blocked kick had saved three points briefly. The turnover returned them before halftime. The Bulwark went to the break trailing 20–0, with no scoring possession of their own.
Six targets, six catches is the standard I wanted today. The third downs are the part I care about. If the ball comes my way there, I expect us to keep playing.
body.speaker: Scep Smith Jr.

body.text: Fourth down made the lead larger

Gabite began the third quarter with a seven-yard run, then gained ten more before fumbling. Woodson recovered. The running back ultimately finished with eighty-six yards on sixteen carries, an average of 5.4, but productive rushing cannot help the scoreboard when a drive ends by handing the ball away. Canalave had lost its fourth possession through a turnover before the half had settled into a rhythm.

Mt. Silver used ten plays and forty-eight yards to turn that recovery into another touchdown. Vibrava did much of the ground work, including an eleven-yard run and a four-yard conversion on third-and-three. The series eventually reached fourth-and-two. McLarren kept the offense on, and Thorpe threw short right to Tentacool for an eight-yard score with 3:24 left in the third quarter. Venutieri's extra point went in off the upright. At 27–0, even the narrow successes belonged to the visitors.

Tentacool finished with three catches for fifty yards. Two went for twenty-one yards; the third was that fourth-down touchdown. It was an economical afternoon in the best sense. Gyarzalez later provided a thirty-eight-yard deep-left catch on third-and-ten, moving the Reds close enough for Thorpe to finish from one yard out with 3:05 left. Their final touchdown required another difficult conversion before the short scoring play. The easy-looking end came after the hard part had already been completed.

Canalave did have defenders worth separating from the final score. Delcatty recorded all three sacks of Thorpe, including consecutive seven-yard losses early in the fourth quarter. Weezing made eleven tackles and forced a fumble. Froslass blocked a kick. Those contributions are real. They also underline how little offensive help arrived: Slowking finished eight-of-fifteen for sixty-three passing yards, with one interception, and the Bulwark never attempted a field goal.

The Reds' running totals were less spectacular than their passing ones, but they supplied enough help. Vibrava carried eleven times for forty-seven yards; Raticate added thirty-seven on eleven carries. They did not need to win the game by themselves. Their job was to keep possessions useful around Thorpe's completions, and Vibrava's third-and-three conversion on the third-quarter touchdown drive was a particularly clear example. The Reds could ask several different players for the next small piece.

The health report gives both teams work beyond the score. Jenings is out two weeks for Mt. Silver, taking a productive receiver out of the next matchup. Canalave linebacker Octillery is out six weeks. The Reds have other receivers who contributed here, but losing a player who caught all three targets is still an unwelcome item on McLarren's winning itinerary.

Byron's team fell to 6–4 and sixth in the current Hoenn–Sinnoh playoff order. It visits Olivine next. Mt. Silver remains the first Kanto–Johto seed and hosts a 6–3 Eterna team that has allowed seventy-seven points through nine games. That meeting offers a more interesting question than whether the Reds remembered how to play after the bye. They answered that one quickly. Canalave's final score was zero, and its four turnovers had supplied Mt. Silver twenty points before the last touchdown ever arrived.

articles.title: Hobbes gave Lavender a head start. Pastoria kept the ball moving.
articles.dek: A 76-yard punt return supplied the Wails’ only touchdown in a 17–7 loss. Togekiss and Farigiraf helped Pastoria end a five-game skid while Lavender dropped its fourth straight.
articles.author: ellis-quill

body.text: For a little while, Lavender had the kind of gift a struggling team hopes will change the afternoon. Hobbes fielded a punt at the Wails' twenty-four and returned it seventy-six yards for a touchdown. The defense had already recovered a fumble. A road game against another team searching for a win had begun with Lavender ahead, its returner doing the long-distance work and its offense being asked only to contribute something useful alongside him.

The offense never scored. Pastoria won 17–7, ending a five-game losing streak and sending the Wails to their fourth consecutive defeat. Lavender fell to 4–5 and outside the current seven Kanto–Johto playoff places. Pastoria improved to 3–6. Neither record invites extravagant conclusions, but this was an afternoon when one team found enough connected plays to change its recent story and the other kept finding isolated reasons to hope.

Togekiss completed twenty of twenty-nine passes for 230 yards, one touchdown and no interceptions. Farigiraf caught six for eighty-nine yards and the touchdown that finally gave the Waves a two-score lead. Lavender's Mr. Clanky finished nine-of-twenty-six for ninety-six yards, no touchdowns and one interception. The Wails converted one of nine third downs. I can be patient about a season without pretending those numbers describe a functioning afternoon.

Seventy-six yards is a nice number to have attached to your name. I'd trade the interesting number for a boring win. We had plenty of game left after that return, and we needed something else to happen.
body.speaker: Hobbes

body.text: The early lead asked for a companion

Pastoria's opening possession ended when Watchog fumbled on a five-yard run right, with Picasso recovering for Lavender. The Wails immediately had a chance to turn the takeaway into points. Diggersby lost a yard, then Mr. Clanky threw two incompletions toward Beedrill. Just a cactus punted into the end zone. It was the first example of a pattern that became harder to excuse as the game continued: the defense could create a chance, but the offense still had to do something with it.

The Waves went three plays before punting on their next possession. Hobbes supplied the return touchdown, and Just a cactus added the extra point. Lavender led 7–0. A seventy-six-yard scoring run through a punt return is a major contribution on its own terms. It does not become less impressive because the offense later failed. It does become lonely on the scoring summary.

Lavender's defense forced another punt after Parasect sacked Togekiss for seven yards. The offense then produced its most encouraging early stretch, a nine-play possession that gained sixty yards. Diggersby had a twelve-yard run; Mr. Clanky added runs of seven and eight. Beedrill caught a fifteen-yard short-right pass, and Carnivine contributed on the ground and through the air. There was a recognizable sequence here, enough different pieces moving together to suggest the early lead might acquire some substance.

It ended on the first play after a short Carnivine completion opened the second quarter. Mr. Clanky threw deep left and Dubwool intercepted with 5:39 remaining in the half. Pastoria took over and drove eighty yards in twelve plays. Deerling finished with a three-yard run up the middle at the two-minute warning. Horsea's extra point tied the game. Lavender's best sustained early possession had become the beginning of Pastoria's best sustained early possession.

We got the return, we got the takeaway, and we had a drive where we were moving it. Those were chances to build the game we wanted. We didn't finish enough of them, and we can't keep asking the defense and return game to cover that.
body.speaker: Travis Scarboro

body.text: Pastoria found the passes its run game could not provide

The Waves' tying drive illustrates why the final passing difference mattered. Farigiraf caught passes of seven, sixteen and eleven yards during the possession. Kilowattrel added eleven. Other completions went to Watchog, Phanpy and Seel. Deerling's three-yard touchdown was the finishing touch, but a succession of completed throws had done much of the traveling. Pastoria did not need a dominant rushing afternoon to assemble a complete scoring drive.

It did not have one. Watchog carried fourteen times for twenty-nine yards. The Waves finished with forty-two rushing yards on twenty-three attempts, including Togekiss' kneels. Lavender's front repeatedly made running difficult. Mauler Twin recorded four tackles and two for loss, while Gumshoos and Stunfisk each made five tackles. Those efforts helped keep the score tied at halftime. They were useful work, not a complete solution to an offense stuck on seven points.

Pastoria's receivers gave Togekiss more reliable alternatives. Arbok caught four of five targets for seventy yards. Kilowattrel caught all five targets for thirty-six. Farigiraf's six receptions came on eight targets. Across the field, Beedrill caught three of twelve for twenty-seven yards, while Samurott had no catches on five targets. Those are not verdicts on the players' seasons or careers. They are the routes this particular game offered and the starkly different results they produced.

There were throws we needed and didn't complete. The interception ended a drive that was working. I don't have a better description than that. We have to make the next down easier, and today we kept leaving ourselves the hard one.
body.speaker: Mr. Clanky

body.text: Three failed fourth downs closed the remaining doors

The second half began with Lavender trying to take control of a manageable situation. Diggersby gained three yards, lost one, and Mr. Clanky found Beedrill for seven. On fourth-and-one, the quarterback ran right and Aggron stopped him for no gain. Pastoria took over, moved sixteen yards and kicked a thirty-yard field goal. Horsea had given the Waves their first lead, 10–7, with 3:49 left in the third quarter.

Lavender still had time, and its defense continued to supply opportunities. Pastoria later tried fourth-and-one itself, throwing incomplete toward Gumshoos. The Wails took possession and began a fifty-yard drive. Frosmoth caught a twenty-seven-yard deep-left pass. People Eater added fourteen on third-and-five. Those were substantial gains in a game where Lavender finished with only 160 total yards. Once again, there was enough movement to make the ending particularly frustrating.

The final three plays of that possession gained three yards: a short completion to Luvdisc, a Diggersby run for no gain, and an incomplete fourth-and-seven throw to Beedrill as the fourth quarter began. Lavender remained within a field goal. It also remained unable to convert its more promising stretches into even that field goal. A team can spend a long time within reach while steadily using up the possessions required to reach anything.

Pincurchin then helped make the next Wails possession brief. Mr. Clanky's deep-right throw to Samurott was broken up by Pincurchin, a short-left attempt to Samurott was broken up by Arctibax, and a deep-left throw to Frosmoth was broken up by Pincurchin. Three incompletions, three recorded breakups, another punt. The Waves' defense did not need a sack to produce a clean stop. Pincurchin finished with three pass breakups; Appletun added two.

Pastoria finally created separation with seven plays and eighty-seven yards. Farigiraf gained fifteen short right. Gumshoos caught fourteen on second-and-twelve. Arbok added twenty-one down the left side. With 2:28 remaining, Togekiss threw short left to Farigiraf, who gained thirty-one yards and scored. Horsea made the extra point. The Waves led 17–7, and Lavender now needed two scoring possessions from an offense that had not produced one.
I enjoyed the short pass becoming the long problem. We'd kept finding enough to move, and that one finally gave us some room. I wasn't interested in giving them another close ending.
body.speaker: Farigiraf

body.text: Lavender's last possession ended with its third failed fourth down of the half, a short-right throw to Beedrill broken up by Watchog. Pastoria then used a five-yard Watchog run on third-and-five to reach the kneeling stage. The Waves go to Mahogany next; the Wails host Veilstone, another club needing a response after a loss. There is still room in the season for Lavender to recover. The immediate request is much smaller than a declaration about its future: after Hobbes carries the ball seventy-six yards, someone on offense needs to carry the score beyond seven.

art.alt: Hobbes looks toward the field from a quiet Lavender sideline.

articles.title: Keep the receipt: Mossdeep survives, Rustboro earns the upgrade
articles.dek: The top four hold, the Stone jump to fifth, and Sootopolis finally supplies a win worth arguing about. Rowan Vale audits all 32 teams after Week 10.
articles.author: rowan-vale

body.text: Mossdeep won by three. Mt. Silver won by thirty-four. Both are 9–0, and I am leaving the Eclipse first because a narrow win over Saffron is still a better answer than pretending the opponent does not matter. Dorian has been invited to express his disagreement at a volume appropriate for a building with other occupants.

This week every club brings a receipt: one result or absence that supports the rank, complicates it, or makes me revise last week. Rustboro climbs past Cinnabar after beating it. Sootopolis makes the largest jump. Previous positions are the ones actually published, not the more flattering versions I might remember. These are power rankings; the standings retain their own perfectly functional arithmetic.

rankings.themeLabel: Receipt: a win when twenty was enough.
rankings.text: Last week I wanted an examination. Saffron provided one, and Mossdeep passed 20–17 without receiving extra credit for artistic presentation. Dram Marino threw two touchdowns to Accel BeckhmJr; the offense survived four sacks. Nine wins still buy first place here. Marshall Flock's five-week absence is a serious new bill, especially with a trip to Vermilion next. The Eclipse have proved they can win a close one. Now they must prove they can keep winning with another job to cover.

rankings.themeLabel: Receipt: thirty-four to absolutely nothing.
rankings.text: The Reds stayed second while Canalave's offense stayed silent. Tic Thorpe threw for 281 yards and three touchdowns, ran for another, and Mt. Silver reached 9–0 with a 34–0 win. The Reds keep finding ways to win while the weekly explanation changes. That is a much better kind of repetition than another narrow escape. Eterna arrives next with a defense allowing 77 points through nine games. That is a much more interesting test than arguing about my stationery.

rankings.themeLabel: Receipt: the favorite had to work.
rankings.text: I picked Saffron to win. It lost by three, and I am somehow more convinced that third is the correct address. Archam Manning produced 258 passing yards, Gengar Pickens had 107 receiving, and a defense missing Verrick Brooks still sacked Marino four times. The 7–2 Psi Corps have allowed seventy points all season. They must finish the next close opportunity, of course. But a narrow loss to No. 1 does not require me to pretend they became ordinary.

rankings.themeLabel: Receipt: the win counts; the warning does too.
rankings.text: The Dragons remain fourth after escaping Hearthome 27–25. Hatterene completed seventeen of twenty-one for 249 yards and two touchdowns, which remains an excellent way to discourage panic. Forty-nine rushing yards and a two-point margin make the rest of the report less serene. Blackthorn is 8–1, with Sunyshore next and Grovyle now absent six weeks. I requested portable control last week. Clair returned with a win and a bag containing several loose screws.

rankings.themeLabel: Receipt: the passing game has entered the meeting.
rankings.text: Up three. Last week I praised the backs; this week Porygon-Z threw five touchdowns and Gibby Timmy caught three of them in a 41–38 win over Cinnabar. A developing team is allowed more than one answer. The 6–4 Stone enter their bye with My Way, Son carrying a one-week absence and a defense that would appreciate fewer emergency assignments. Still, beating the team above you is a persuasive way to request its chair.

rankings.themeLabel: Receipt: seven wins, with the next one still unearned.
rankings.text: Unchanged at sixth through the bye, which will disappoint anyone hoping I would penalize the Starseekers for resting efficiently. Sunyshore is 7–2 and plus-109. Blackthorn away is the next assignment, with Myles Gabite still out three weeks. Karson Jones has had time to prepare; Clair has just survived a two-point game. I expect a proper contender's contest. My personal preference for Sunyshore losing remains separate from recognizing what a road win would mean.

rankings.themeLabel: Receipt: thirty-eight points and an empty return trip.
rankings.text: Down two after 41–38 at Rustboro. I still like the 7–3 Blaze, and Gholdengo's 325 passing yards support that affection. Allowing five passing touchdowns supports a much less pleasant conversation. Last week I asked whether the defense could stop Rustboro's runners; the Stone answered by changing the examination paper. Cinnabar's bye is useful. Blaine should use it to ensure the next opponent cannot make one receiving target feel like three separate emergencies.

rankings.themeLabel: Receipt: the offense keeps contributing.
rankings.text: Down one only because Rustboro jumped the queue. Eterna beat Azalea 27–13, Stantler ran for 140 yards, and the team allowed twenty-five rushing yards while collecting four sacks. At 6–3, the Thorns now have a plus-49 differential and an offense that has stopped requiring a formal invitation to help. Mt. Silver is next. That will tell us more than another comfortable ranking paragraph, although I have generously supplied this one anyway.

rankings.themeLabel: Receipt: an unglamorous recovery still spends.
rankings.text: The Pride stay ninth after beating Viridian 14–7. Iron Valiant threw two touchdowns, Oinkologne ran for seventy-five yards, and the defense allowed 191 total rushing-plus-passing yards. Norman's club is 6–3. Last week's Cinnabar loss did not demand an identity crisis; it demanded a response. This qualifies. Pewter away offers another defensive contest, where fourteen points may again be useful and seventeen would represent an encouraging interest in personal growth.

rankings.themeLabel: Receipt: two wins, and this one came with zero allowed.
rankings.text: Up three after a 14–0 win at Snowpoint. Olivine has followed its own shutout loss with victories of 29–10 and 14–0, a sequence that suggests the embarrassment was at least put to work. Drampa completed twenty of twenty-five. The 5–4 Ironclads still carry a minus-two differential and several lengthy injuries, so I am withholding the brass band. Canalave visits next with no points from its last game. Keep the welcome brief.

rankings.themeLabel: Receipt: the overtime escape remains on file.
rankings.text: Unchanged during the bye at 5–4. Ambipom's 175 scrimmage yards against Viridian have not depreciated merely because another week happened. Neither have the two turnovers that made that overtime escape necessary. Dewford visits a Celadon team coming off six points and 99 passing yards. I want a clean road win before I move my favorite occasional headache any higher. A contender should sometimes leave the dramatic late field goal in its packaging.

rankings.themeLabel: Receipt: fourteen is more than six.
rankings.text: Up two after a third consecutive win, 14–6 at Veilstone. Iron Jugulis threw two touchdowns, Furret supplied eighty-three receiving yards, and the defense kept another opponent out of double figures. The 5–4 Falcons are still minus-fourteen for the season. Fine: recent improvement and an imperfect past can coexist. Hearthome visits next with an offense that just scored twenty-five against Blackthorn. Violet may have to increase the scoring budget from pocket change to actual notes.

rankings.themeLabel: Receipt: six wins do not erase the minus sign.
rankings.text: Down one after losing 24–10 at Sootopolis. The Volts are 6–3 and now minus-six, having allowed Drampa to throw three touchdowns without a sack or interception. Last week's narrow surplus has expired. Mossdeep arrives next, and Vermilion's lengthy cornerback absences have not acquired a convenient exception for unbeaten visitors. Chandelure needs more than 160 passing yards; the defense needs to make the opposing quarterback notice it exists. Preferably before the postgame handshake.

rankings.themeLabel: Receipt: three sacks, no points.
rankings.text: Down four after 34–0 against Mt. Silver. Delcatty produced three sacks, Gabite ran for eighty-six yards, and Canalave still managed only sixty-three passing yards. The Bulwark are 6–4 with a minus-21 differential. Last week I wondered how long the defense could survive a small offensive cushion. This time somebody removed the cushion entirely. A trip to Olivine follows. Byron needs scoring possessions, not another earnest explanation of how difficult the opponent was.

rankings.themeLabel: Receipt: the recovery has reached three games.
rankings.text: Up three after beating Cerulean 17–9. Fortree is still 3–6, but a three-game winning streak carries rather more weight than the original pleasant surprise. Floatzel ran for eighty-four yards, Dunsparce caught eight passes, and the defense allowed twenty-five rushing yards. Saffron away is next. The Skyhawks will need more than momentum there, but Winona has earned the right to arrive with an argument instead of an apology.

rankings.themeLabel: Receipt: the quarterback had time and used it.
rankings.text: Up eleven, because beating a 6–2 visitor 24–10 deserves more than a reluctant nod. Drampa completed twenty of twenty-six for 233 yards and three touchdowns without taking a sack. Sootopolis is 4–5 and still minus-58, so the season has not suddenly become beautiful. The latest game did. Fuchsia is next, offering Wallace an opportunity to make competence repeatable. I would like a second receipt before we discuss store credit for earlier losses.

rankings.themeLabel: Receipt: a tie remains a tie through a bye.
rankings.text: Up two while idle because several neighbors actively damaged their applications. Mahogany is 3–5–1 with a plus-fourteen differential. That combination still interests me more than the record alone. Kricketune remains out ten weeks, and Pastoria arrives having found a productive passing afternoon. Pryce's team must turn competitive football into complete wins. I can move it a little on others' mistakes; the Frost should not build their playoff plan around my generosity.

rankings.themeLabel: Receipt: another close game, another missing win.
rankings.text: Up two after losing 27–25 to Blackthorn. The Haunts are 3–6–1, and yes, that is still a poor record. They also scored twenty-five against an 8–1 team, with Frosmoth throwing two touchdowns and the defense allowing forty-nine rushing yards. Fantina has made the games competitive. Winning them remains the next item. Violet is a useful test: a tight defensive team that will not award points for being more troublesome than expected.

rankings.themeLabel: Receipt: defense has kept the season open.
rankings.text: Up two through the bye at 4–5. Pewter has scored seventy-seven points, which would be an acceptable weekend if it did not represent nine games. The defense has kept the Rockers close enough to remain relevant. Petalburg visits with a similar appetite for a low-scoring result, but Brock still has two cornerbacks facing long absences. I want the offense to contribute before the defense submits an invoice. Dorian's museum joke is already overdrawn.

rankings.themeLabel: Receipt: seventeen was a substantial improvement.
rankings.text: Up nine after a 17–7 win over Lavender. Togekiss threw for 230 yards without an interception, Farigiraf supplied eighty-nine receiving yards, and the defense held Mr. Clanky to nine completions. The Waves are 3–6. I asked for another scoring drive last week; Pastoria supplied enough of an afternoon to earn the request's retirement. Mahogany away comes next, where the opposing record is less impressive than its differential. Keep the useful passing game packed.

rankings.themeLabel: Receipt: the air route worked.
rankings.text: Up four for 24–6 against Celadon. Togekiss threw for 238 yards and two touchdowns; Mothim caught eight passes. Fourteen rushing yards are less persuasive, but I will not demand balance before acknowledging that Mauville actually finished with twenty-four points. The 4–6 Dynamos enter their bye with something to build from. Last week's three-point showing remains evidence of the floor. This week's passing gives Wattson a reasonable direction toward a less embarrassing ceiling.

rankings.themeLabel: Receipt: another close loss is still a loss.
rankings.text: Down seven after 14–7 at Petalburg. Viridian is 4–6, having followed the overtime loss to Dewford with 118 passing yards and one touchdown. The defense kept the game available; the offense did not buy it. Toucannon, Sneasel and now Bonsly are among the players facing absences. The bye gives Giovanni time to reassess an attack that keeps leaving the final margin too small. Competitiveness without finishing is becoming a very repetitive product description.

rankings.themeLabel: Receipt: nine points will not repair fifty-six allowed.
rankings.text: Down seven after 17–9 at Fortree. Cerulean's defense improved enormously from the Mossdeep disaster; the offense answered with twenty-five rushing yards and one touchdown pass in forty-five attempts. The Tide are 4–5. Arctozolt's eighty-nine receiving yards are useful, but they need company on the scoreboard. Lavaridge visits next. Misty should welcome the opportunity without confusing the Inferno's season totals with permission to repeat this week's finishing.

rankings.themeLabel: Receipt: a defensive result worth keeping.
rankings.text: Up four after beating Fuchsia 21–7. Lavaridge has allowed 234 points in nine games, and seven of them arrived this week. That contrast is the whole reason for the climb. Delphox threw two touchdowns, and the Inferno are 3–6 with a trip to Cerulean next. Flannery finally received enough resistance from the defense to make useful offense count. Repeat it once more and we can stop introducing every compliment with the season's alarming total.

rankings.themeLabel: Receipt: four touchdown passes, seventy-eight passing yards.
rankings.text: Up six after winning 28–17 at Oreburgh. Victreebel's line is a direct challenge to anybody who sorts quarterbacks by yardage and stops reading: four touchdowns on seventy-eight yards. Swampert ran for ninety-two. Cianwood is 3–7, Gardevoir is still out seven weeks, and one productive result does not solve the season. It does disprove last week's suggestion that the available offense had nothing useful to offer. Snowpoint visits next. Keep making me revise that paragraph.

rankings.themeLabel: Receipt: nine completions do not sustain a playoff argument.
rankings.text: Down nine after a 17–7 loss at Pastoria. Mr. Clanky went nine-for-twenty-six for ninety-six yards and an interception. Lavender is 4–5 with a minus-85 differential. I have spent weeks discussing second halves; this result makes the whole offense the subject. Veilstone visits next, another team struggling to score. Travis Scarboro needs a convincing response, because winning an argument about which offense is less broken would still be a very modest achievement.

rankings.themeLabel: Receipt: twenty-five rushing yards and four sacks allowed.
rankings.text: Down five after losing 27–13 at Eterna. Azalea is 4–6 and has followed a shutout loss with another afternoon in which sustained offense was difficult. Doduo remains out four weeks. The Swarm host Oreburgh next, a chance to improve against a defense that just allowed four touchdown passes on remarkably little passing yardage. Bugsy must turn that opportunity into an actual result. The schedule cannot complete a third down on the team's behalf.

rankings.themeLabel: Receipt: the defense cannot score every point itself.
rankings.text: Down five after losing 14–6 to Violet. Tatsugiri threw for 183 yards but no touchdowns and two interceptions. Veilstone is 4–6, with a trip to Lavender next. The Fists keep finding games in which ordinary offensive assistance would make the outcome plausible. They keep failing to provide it. Maylene does not need an extravagant attack to reverse this pattern. She needs one that can see a fourteen-point opponent and consider the number negotiable.

rankings.themeLabel: Receipt: no touchdowns, no field goals, no ambiguity.
rankings.text: Down five after a 14–0 home loss to Olivine. Snowpoint is 2–7 and minus-twenty-six. The old argument that the Blizzard were better than their record remains possible, but it is becoming harder to deliver with a straight face. Forty-six rushing yards and 130 passing yards did not threaten enough. Cianwood is next, fresh from a surprisingly efficient win. Candice must find scoring before I run out of synonyms for competitive-looking defeat.

rankings.themeLabel: Receipt: the replacement offense needed more help.
rankings.text: Down four after 24–6 at Mauville. Infernape threw for ninety-nine yards, while Seaking's seventy-six rushing yards were the more useful part of a 2–8 team's afternoon. The Bloom's defense allowed only fourteen rushing yards and still conceded twenty-four points. Dewford visits after its bye, so stopping one department will not be enough. Erika needs a more complete answer. The injured secondary and recent quarterback disruption explain difficulty; they do not make six points adequate.

rankings.themeLabel: Receipt: the useful yards came with costly mistakes.
rankings.text: Down one after losing 28–17 to Cianwood. Furret had 137 receiving yards, Diggersby ran for seventy-seven, and Cryogonal threw two interceptions. The Miners are 2–8. I will not pretend the yardage was meaningless, but I also cannot cash it for a win Roark did not get. Azalea away gives Oreburgh another opponent searching for a repair. Protecting the ball would be an excellent place to begin, before the same explanation becomes a franchise slogan.

rankings.themeLabel: Receipt: one win, ten games.
rankings.text: Unchanged at thirty-second after 21–7 at Lavaridge. Empoleon threw for 212 yards without a touchdown, and Fuchsia is now 1–9. The Shadows have managed to make several opponents feel considerably better about themselves. Sootopolis arrives next after its own convincing passing performance. Koga needs points and stops in the same game, preferably in sufficient quantities to affect the result. There is room to climb. At this position, that is less encouragement than geometry.

articles.title: The Rook Board: Iron Bundle gets first chase
articles.dek: Two Throhs, two Octillery prospects, one Hoenn favorite and a stopwatch worth a second look. Calvin Rook ranks twelve linebackers by the jobs he wants to investigate.
articles.author: calvin-rook

body.text: There are at least two very different linebacker conversations happening in this league. Saffron is replacing the injured Verrick Brooks, whose thirteen sacks still lead everyone. Canalave is trying to turn pressure into a complete defensive afternoon while dealing with absences inside. Mossdeep just got three sacks in a close win. Saying a team needs a linebacker is the beginning of a scouting discussion, not a sufficient job description.

Last week I worked through the defensive line. This week I am separating the fast outside invitation from the interior assignment, then taking responsibility for a few preferences. Iron Bundle goes above the strongest displayed range. Bouffalant gets the warmth of my Lilycove affection and a place he still has to defend. These are early scouting opinions from visible ranges, age, level and combine measurements; no college production or hidden traits are being smuggled into the argument.

The ranges are broad, and their upper endpoints are not current ratings. A forty measures a run; it does not establish recognition. A bench test supplies context; it does not certify a block defeat. I want the numbers translated into questions that actual scouting can answer. The board can move when those answers arrive. Until then, here are twelve individual prospects, with school names kept distinct even where the species repeat.

prospects.name: Iron Bundle
prospects.analysis: I am putting Iron Bundle first, ahead of the highest displayed range, because the movement case is unusually persuasive. Shalour's outside linebacker brings a 4.53 forty, a 47-inch vertical and a 5.96 cone alongside a 69–97 range. That combination makes me want to investigate the space between edge pressure and pursuit, rather than assign one narrow job from a species name. Saffron's Verrick Brooks has shown what disruptive linebacker production can mean to a season. The comparison is an ambition, not thirteen sacks written into a draft card.
prospects.concern: Seventeen bench reps do not settle his ability to handle blockers, and testing numbers do not demonstrate recognition or coverage decisions.
prospects.projection: My first linebacker to investigate. Fortree should make room in its scouting schedule; rebuilding a defense needs players who can reach more than one problem.

prospects.name: Throh
prospects.analysis: Agate State's Throh has the strongest visible range on this board at 71–99. He is twenty-three, level sixteen, and his 5.05 forty and 7.02 cone suggest a different conversation from Iron Bundle's. I want to see the interior responsibilities: closing a lane, taking the correct angle, finishing a stop before an ordinary gain becomes a first down. That is less glamorous than declaring a pass-rush savior and often more useful. Throh is my best starting point for that investigation.
prospects.concern: The upper endpoint is not a present rating. His testing does not justify assuming he can cover every outside assignment as easily as an interior one.
prospects.projection: An early inside-linebacker target. Canalave's current absences make the long-term middle of the defense a sensible scouting subject.

prospects.name: Qwilfish
prospects.analysis: Qwilfish gives Mid-Galar State a credible challenger near the top: 67–95, a 4.81 forty, a 41-inch vertical and a 6.42 cone. I like the broad movement invitation. It is not Iron Bundle's spectacular card, but it does not need to be. My first question is whether he can keep his pursuit under control when the runner changes the destination. My second is how much useful work he can do when an offense refuses to let him rush cleanly.
prospects.concern: Seventeen bench reps and a fast drill do not tell us how consistently he defeats contact. The actual football responsibilities still require scouting.
prospects.projection: An early outside-linebacker option. Lavender should investigate a defender who could help end possessions, rather than simply hope the offense makes them shorter.

prospects.name: Bouffalant
prospects.analysis: I am moving Lilycove's Bouffalant above a few higher ranges. There: the Hoenn affection is declared. The 63–91 range is substantial, and twenty bench reps with a 4.96 forty give the interior case a useful physical outline. At twenty-one and level thirteen, he is also younger than Agate's Throh. I want him assessed in traffic, where strength, balance and choosing the correct gap need to become one decision. The stopwatch is a reason to watch, not permission to stop watching.
prospects.concern: A 6.96 cone is not evidence of effortless coverage. Younger age leaves possibilities; it does not promise a faster development rate.
prospects.projection: My preferred interior alternative after Throh. Fortree and Mauville should compare his actual assignments with their needs before treating another edge athlete as the universal answer.

prospects.name: Throh
prospects.analysis: The University of Mahogany's Throh makes a good argument for keeping identical species on separate scouting pages. This one is twenty-one, level eleven, with a 65–93 range and twenty bench reps. The 5.07 forty and 7.04 cone are close to Agate's figures, while the visible range is lower. I would not collapse those differences into one generic 'Throh prospect.' His individual report could support a different price and a different timetable.
prospects.concern: The lower level cannot tell us how quickly he will improve. Similar combine times do not prove he is interchangeable with the prospect ranked second.
prospects.projection: A serious inside-linebacker candidate. Teams weighing an immediate foundation against a longer project should scout both Throhs, then make the comparison with actual information.

prospects.name: Mawile
prospects.analysis: Cyllage's Mawile has a 62–90 range, a 4.98 forty and a 6.89 cone. I like this as the point on the board where a team can stop chasing the most spectacular testing card and start asking about a specific outside job. The thirty-five-inch vertical is useful context; fourteen bench reps make the contact question unavoidable. He is twenty-one and level fourteen. Give me the player who can reliably perform the assignment a coordinator actually needs, not the best imaginary combination of everybody's numbers.
prospects.concern: Nothing in these measurements proves the ability to anchor against a larger blocker or diagnose an unfolding route combination.
prospects.projection: A scouting priority for a team seeking a complementary outside defender. Lavender should demand a clear intended job before adding another interesting name.

prospects.name: Sableye
prospects.analysis: Porto Marinada Coastal's Sableye shares Mawile's 62–90 range but brings a different set of tests: 5.07 in the forty, fourteen bench reps and a 6.96 cone. I prefer Mawile's movement card narrowly; I am keeping Sableye close enough that a better football evaluation could reverse them. At twenty-one and level eighteen, he has an intriguing visible starting point. This is where a scout should earn an opinion, rather than simply sort by one hundredth of a second.
prospects.concern: The combine does not establish anticipation, tackling reliability or how the player handles a failed first move. Those are questions, not assumed weaknesses.
prospects.projection: A middle-board outside option with room to climb. Mauville should compare the work he can actually perform with the more athletic alternatives, not draft a ranking number.

prospects.name: Pyukumuku
prospects.analysis: Ambrette Naval's Pyukumuku is my deliberate disagreement with a straight range sort. The 64–92 range is strong, but the 5.23 forty, fourteen bench reps and 7.17 cone leave me with more questions about the breadth of the interior assignment. He is twenty-one and level eight. I can imagine a useful focused role; I cannot use imagination as evidence. I want this player scouted carefully enough that the eventual decision is about his football, not the novelty of the name.
prospects.concern: The visible level is low and the movement measurements are modest. Neither establishes hidden potential, but both make an assumed all-purpose role premature.
prospects.projection: An interior prospect worth deeper work before a firm grade. Teams comfortable developing a specific role should investigate; teams needing immediate universal cover should resist shortcuts.

prospects.name: Octillery
prospects.analysis: Violet's Octillery brings the more advanced visible level in this part of the board: twenty-five, with a 61–89 range at age twenty-two. Eighteen bench reps, a 5.02 forty and a 7.05 cone give a reasonably balanced testing outline without the striking outside athleticism of the leaders. I would begin with repeatable inside work. The league already has several Octillery linebackers collecting sacks, but sharing a species is not a substitute for assessing this individual.
prospects.concern: Level twenty-five is not proof of professional readiness, and existing players' sack totals do not transfer to a prospect with the same face.
prospects.projection: An inside-linebacker comparison point for clubs preferring a more developed visible starting level. Scout the role before deciding that the higher level deserves the higher pick.

prospects.name: Octillery
prospects.analysis: Cherrygrove's Octillery is twenty-three and also level twenty-five. His 59–87 range is slightly lower than Violet's, with nineteen bench reps and a thirty-six-inch vertical. I find that a useful comparison: broadly similar starting profiles, different individual evidence, and no reason to pretend one drill settles the order. The 5.05 forty and 7.03 cone keep the interior discussion more convincing than an expansive chase-everything promise.
prospects.concern: A marginal advantage in bench or vertical is not a complete player advantage. His older age and the lower range belong in the same comparison.
prospects.projection: A practical interior scouting alternative. Clubs shopping in this part of the board should compare both Octillery prospects rather than assume the school name is the difference.

prospects.name: Castform
prospects.analysis: Medali's Castform is my movement wildcard: 4.91 in the forty, a thirty-eight-inch vertical and a 6.70 cone. The 56–84 range trails the players above, and at twenty-three with level seven there is no honest basis for calling this a ready-made solution. I still want the next look. A defense with a defined outside task may find the athletic outline more interesting than a broader but slower profile. I am asking for evidence, while admitting I already like the invitation.
prospects.concern: Thirteen bench reps leave the contact question open. The low level, age and lower range require a sober price rather than an excited promise.
prospects.projection: My outside watch-list choice. Fortree should investigate the movement; it should not confuse my enthusiasm with a guarantee that the development timetable fits.

prospects.name: Pincurchin
prospects.analysis: Pewter's Pincurchin closes the dozen with a 59–87 range and eighteen bench reps. The 5.19 forty and 7.19 cone make this a narrower athletic case, but I do not want every linebacker discussion reduced to finding another Iron Bundle. At twenty-two and level twenty, there is a useful question about an inside role and the consistency needed to perform it. The answer must come from scouting the player, not apologizing for his stopwatch.
prospects.concern: The movement measurements make an expansive pursuit or coverage projection hard to justify from current information. A bounded role still has to be demonstrated.
prospects.projection: A focused inside-linebacker study. A team seeking dependable interior depth should investigate the fundamentals before paying for an upside story the visible evidence has not told.

articles.title: Fine, Wallace. Now do it again.
articles.dek: Sootopolis gave Drampa a clean game and Vermilion a 24–10 defeat. Mara Voss can admire the work without declaring the Surge repaired.
articles.author: mara-voss

body.text: I have spent enough time being irritated by Sootopolis that I should probably acknowledge a good afternoon when the Surge finally arrange one. Here it is: Drampa completed twenty of twenty-six passes for 233 yards, threw three touchdowns, threw no interceptions and took no sacks. Wallace's team beat a six-win opponent 24–10. Those are substantial things. I will even put them before the complaints.

The complaints are still coming. Sootopolis is 4–5, has allowed 204 points in nine games, and arrived here after scoring nine against Violet and seven against Saffron. One efficient passing performance doesn't fill those holes. It does establish a standard that the coach can now be asked to repeat. My argument is simple: Wallace should build the next week around the decisions that kept this offense functioning, rather than treat the win as permission to forget why it had stopped.

There is a temptation to call any three-touchdown quarterback performance an explosion. I prefer the smaller, more useful description. Drampa kept producing completions without paying the usual tax in backward plays and turnovers. Sootopolis finished with 233 passing yards and 74 rushing yards. The ground game helped, but it did not need to turn into something unrecognizable for the passing game to work. That matters for an offense whose season has already supplied plenty of unsuccessful afternoons.
We can throw it. Put that in the first sentence. Then put in the part where we have to do it next week, because I'm tired of explaining the week before.
body.speaker: Drampa

body.text: That is the appropriate impatience. Drampa's season line now reads 1,969 yards, sixteen touchdowns and seven interceptions. The ability to move the ball has existed alongside the inconsistency. Against Vermilion, he completed almost seventy-seven percent of his attempts. His twenty completions came from only twenty-six throws. The goal isn't to expect that exact percentage every week. It is to stop behaving as if a workable possession requires a spectacular rescue.
Give the quarterback more than one useful answer

Arbok led the receiving work with five catches for 67 yards and a touchdown. Rillaboom added three for 44 and a score. Seaking caught four for 34 and another touchdown; Pawmo supplied four for 29. The opening possession of the second half explains why that variety mattered. Down 10–3, Sootopolis converted third-and-one with a short-right throw to Rillaboom that became a 37-yard gain. Later in the same possession, Drampa found Arbok deep left for eighteen on third-and-nine. Finally, on third-and-three, he went short left to Seaking for the seven-yard touchdown.

Three different third downs. Three different receivers. A short throw with a long result, a downfield completion when the offense actually needed distance, and another short throw to finish. That is what I want Wallace teaching from. The 79-yard drive survived more than one kind of problem. Sootopolis went six-of-nine on third down overall; Vermilion went two-of-ten. The contrast tells us far more than a generic declaration that one team wanted the game more.

That distinction becomes more important with Heatmor still out. The injured tight end is listed with four weeks remaining. Seaking's contribution against Vermilion was therefore worth more than a decorative mention beneath the quarterback's numbers. Four catches and a touchdown are actual help. So are Pawmo's four completions and Magby's two for 23 yards. A receiving group does not have to be famous to prevent a quarterback from running out of answers.

Rillaboom's rushing line was ten carries for 52 yards. Add the receiving work and he contributed 96 yards from scrimmage, with the touchdown arriving through the air. I like that distribution more than I like an argument about whether the Surge were sufficiently committed to running. They received useful work from the back in both phases. Calling another carry merely to improve the balance of a spreadsheet would not automatically improve the offense.
The throws made my job easier, and the blocking gave me room on the runs. I got the numbers, but there were a lot of people making sure I had somewhere to go.
body.speaker: Rillaboom

body.text: He is being generous. He is also describing the right relationship. An offense asks different players to solve different parts of the same possession. On this afternoon, the runner helped the passer and the passer rewarded several receivers. The lack of a sack is especially welcome. Sootopolis has surrendered twelve this season, so a clean passing line deserves attention even without declaring the protection problem permanently solved.
The defense has to keep its share of the agreement

The other number I don't want lost is ten. Vermilion scored ten points, all before halftime. Sootopolis held its rushing production to sixty yards, recorded two sacks and received an interception from Kingdra. The interception came on a deep-right throw immediately after Seaking's tying touchdown. Kingdra returned it twenty-four yards; Drampa then hit Arbok deep right for a 24-yard score on the very next offensive play. One unit created the opportunity and the other cashed it in. No elaborate personality theory required.

The Surge have allowed 22.7 points per game over the season. They had given up thirty-five at Saffron one week earlier. I am not going to build a new defensive reputation from one opponent's ten-point total. I am going to insist that this part of the win belongs in the discussion. Praising the quarterback while letting the defense float away from its responsibilities is how a useful team performance gets turned into a much less useful celebrity profile.
We gave ourselves a game we could manage. The offense finished its opportunities, and the defense made the scoring matter. The next part is showing we can work to that standard again.
body.speaker: Wallace

body.text: Good. Keep the last sentence. I would also keep the final possession. Leading 24–10, the Surge took over with 4:08 left and never gave the ball back. Short completions to Seaking, Arbok and Pawmo preceded useful runs, including Drilbur's five-yard gain on third-and-two. The drive ended with kneels. After three touchdown possessions, the offense finished by removing Vermilion's remaining chance to answer. That is a better definition of control than simply pointing at the score.

Sootopolis has already won consecutive games this season, against Cerulean and Fortree, and then followed its bye with two losses. Momentum has been announced here before. It did not arrive with a warranty. This win should change the week's preparation more than it changes the language on the posters.

The next opponent is Fuchsia, which is 1–9 after losing 21–7 at Lavaridge. That is an opportunity, and the Surge have not earned the right to regard opportunities as formalities. Sootopolis needs another controlled passing performance, another useful afternoon from its receivers and a defense that doesn't require the quarterback to repair every possession. The record still places it outside the current playoff field. There is work available before anyone needs to discuss a ceiling.

I would start the review with the players who made this win specific: Drampa completing twenty throws, Arbok leading the receiving yards, Rillaboom helping twice, Seaking delivering with Heatmor absent, Kingdra ending a possession. Then I would ask what each needs to make the next opponent equally uncomfortable. That is a football meeting. A celebration of the team's newly discovered identity can wait until the identity has survived another week.

Sootopolis doesn't get to erase the previous eight games. It gets to use the ninth. Wallace has a cleaner example to teach from now, and I have fewer reasons to roll my eyes at this particular performance. I consider both developments encouraging. Repeat the useful parts at Fuchsia, and I might even manage a second compliment without needing a running start.
